content: The Haemophilus b conjugate vaccine, HIBERIX, has been associated with certain adverse reactions, as observed in clinical trials and post-marketing reports. Below is a detailed account of these findings: 1. Clinical Trials Experience: Clinical trials are conducted under varying conditions, and the rates of adverse reactions observed in these trials cannot be directly compared to those of other vaccines or to real-world practice. It is possible that broader use of HIBERIX may reveal adverse reactions not identified during clinical trials. Studies involving HIBERIX were conducted in Europe, Canada, and Latin America. The mean age of subjects receiving a booster dose of HIBERIX ranged from 16 to 19 months, with 2% of subjects aged 19 to 25 months. Approximately half of the subjects were male, and nearly all were white. In one open-label, multicenter study in Germany, 371 children received a booster dose of HIBERIX concomitantly with DTaP-HBV-IPV. The mean age at vaccination was 16 months. Subjects had previously received a primary series of either HIBERIX (not approved for primary immunization in the U.S.), a Haemophilus b conjugate vaccine manufactured by Sanofi Pasteur SA, or a vaccine manufactured by Wyeth Pharmaceuticals Inc. (no longer licensed in the U.S.). All subjects had also received three doses of DTaP-HBV-IPV. 2. Solicited Adverse Events: Local reactions at the injection site included redness, swelling, and pain. Grade 3 redness or swelling was defined as >20 mm, and Grade 3 pain was defined as causing crying when the limb was moved. General adverse events included fever (≥39.0°C axillary, oral, or tympanic), fussiness (Grade 3 defined as persistent crying that could not be comforted), and symptoms preventing normal daily activity. 3. Serious Adverse Events: Among 1,008 subjects, two serious adverse events were reported within 31 days following booster immunization with HIBERIX. One subject developed bilateral pneumonia nine days post-vaccination, and another experienced asthenia following accidental drug ingestion 18 days post-vaccination. 4. Post-Marketing Experience: Since the introduction of HIBERIX in 1996, worldwide voluntary reports of adverse events have been collected. These include serious events and those with a plausible causal connection to the vaccine. However, due to the voluntary nature of these reports and the uncertain population size, it is not possible to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a definitive causal relationship to vaccination. 5. Specific Adverse Events: General Disorders and Administration Site Conditions: Extensive swelling of the vaccinated limb and injection site induration. Immune System Disorders: Allergic reactions, including anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions, and angioedema. Nervous System Disorders: Convulsions (with or without fever), hypotonic-hyporesponsive episodes, somnolence, and syncope or vasovagal responses to injection. Respiratory, Thoracic, and Mediastinal Disorders: Apnea. Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue Disorders: Rash and urticaria. This detailed information highlights the potential adverse reactions associated with HIBERIX, emphasizing the importance of monitoring and reporting during both clinical trials and post-marketing surveillance.
